# Education in Nigeria
Education in Nigeria consists of primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, overseen by various government agencies such as the Ministry of Education and the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC). Primary education begins at age 5 and lasts six years, culminating in a first school-leaving certificate. Subjects taught include English, Mathematics, religious and agricultural studies, and indigenous languages. The Universal Primary Education program was established in 1976 and revised several times, eventually leading to the Universal Basic Education (UBE) program in 1999, which made nine years of schooling (six years of primary plus three years of junior secondary) free and compulsory. Promotion between classes is automatic and based on continuous assessment.
Secondary education is a bridge between primary and tertiary levels, divided into three years each of junior (JSS) and senior (SSS) secondary schooling under the "6-3-3-4" or later "9-3-4" systems. Students study a mix of core and elective subjects, and can opt for technical or vocational tracks. Federal, state, and private schools serve different populations, with federal unity schools generally regarded as elite. Teacher qualification requirements exist but are unevenly enforced, and many state-run schools face understaffing and a lack of qualified teachers. Private secondary schools, often costly, offer better facilities and attract more qualified teachers.
Tertiary education includes universities (federal, state, and private), polytechnics, monotechnics, and colleges of education. Admission requires passing national exams such as WAEC or NECO's SSCE, as well as the JAMB entrance exam. Universities are categorized into generations, having grown significantly since independence. Vocational education is available and overseen by the National Board for Technical Education, with additional informal apprenticeship systems encouraged. Despite expansion, challenges persist such as regional literacy disparities, gender inequality due to social barriers, insecure and underfunded schools especially in rural areas, teacher shortages, and political instability affecting literacy and vocational program implementation.
Literacy rates remain low nationwide, with marked regional disparity (especially in northern states), and millions of children remain out of school. While efforts are ongoing—with government and NGO initiatives focused on literacy and female education—progress is hampered by poverty, insecurity, and cultural factors. Notable programs include those aimed at improving female enrollment and retention, such as UNICEF's Girls' Education Project. Nigeria also aims to improve digital literacy, targeting 95% by 2030, to enhance employment and reduce poverty.
